paper_metadata.title: High temperature strength of Mo–Mo3Si–Mo5SiB2 molybdenum silicides

evidence.quote: Ternary and quaternary intermetallic alloys consisting of the phases Mo3Si, Mo5SiB2 (''T2'') and a-Mo (Mo solid solution) were fabricated by melting and casting as well as powder-metallurgy (PM).

Alloys were prepared by arc-melting of elemental starting materials in a partial pressure of argon (70 kPa). The starting materials were typically 99.95% pure (by weight) except for the boron which was 99.5% pure. To achieve homogeneity, the alloys were typically remelted 6 times.
Prior to metallographic examination all cast alloys were annealed for 24 h at 1600/C14Ci n vacuum.

The microstructure in Fig. 6 exhibits a coarse and continuous a-Mo distribution. This particular alloy was fabricated by consolidating Mo–20Si–10B powder particles with their surface regions converted into a-Mo by evaporating Si and SiO in vacuum [9].

The material in Fig. 5 was obtained by mixing Mo–20Si–10B particles with fine (2–8 mm) Mo powder. The micrograph suggests that the bright a-Mo is not fully continuous. However, it is elongated and much coarser than the a-Mo in the cast and annealed alloys.

Alloy PM1 is relatively strong at low temperatures (1200/C14C) whereas it is weak at high temperatures (1400/C14C). In fact, it intersects the other stress-temperature curves in Fig. 9. Qualitatively, the reason for this behavior is its fine microstructure.
The creep strength of pure Mo at 1400/C14Ca n d10/C05 s/C01 is 55 MPa[22].
Fig. 7 shows an engineering stress–strain curve for Mo–12Si–8.5B deformed at 1400/C14C.
After an initial rise the stress reaches a plateau region where it varies only slowly suggesting steady-state creep.
Therefore the creep strength of this alloy at 1200/C14C is similar to that of the coarse-grained alloy PM2.

Tentative support for this argument is found in the relatively low creep strength of alloy PM3 at 1200/C14C (see Fig. 9), which is attributed to the relatively low creep strength of the continuous a-Mo matrix.
Fig. 8 shows that both W and Nb additions cause solid solution strengthening, but the strengthening due to the Nb is much more pronounced.
At low temperatures the effect of the interfaces becomes less important and Hall-Petch hardening may become a factor.

As pointed out by Raj et al., stress exponents near 3 indicate that the creep strength is controlled by viscous dislocation glide. However, the absence of inverse creep in Raj’s silicides [20] and in Mo–12Si–8.5B [8] does not allow one to conclude that viscous dislocation glide is the controlling creep mechanism.
